items.summary: As large language models become stronger, weak supervisors may fail to provide reliable labels, preferences, or final judgments for complex outputs, limiting both weak-to-strong generalization and scalable oversight. We study a more tractable form of weak supervision: using a weak model as a critic rather than as a labeler or judge. Instead of solving the task or selecting the correct answer, the weak critic only needs to provide a non-misleading revision direction that helps the strong model better use its own knowledge. We call this setting *weak-critic strong oversight*. We first show that weak critiques can improve frozen strong models at inference time, and that critique quality is key to this improvement. items.summary: One mode of futurism is estimating the limits of a technology, without regard to what's currently feasible. Whether this is of any relevance to your own generation is another question. Let's consider solar power. Ignoring current technology, it's easy to put a number on the maximum power output. The solar power at the Earth's distance from the sun is called the solar constant. It is 1.36 kW/m². The power on a square meter of the ground is less than that, because of the angle of incidence as well as the atmosphere. The solar constant hasn't changed and technology has, so it's interesting to see how people have reacted to the same number throughout the history of technology. In this post I'll quote both Nikola Tesla and Elon Musk. We'll see that Tesla correctly recognized solar power as a long-term possibility, as well as why it was…

items.summary: We are in AA 9. In Brave New World, Aldous Huxley dated the future from the launch of a car. The book was set in AF 632; AF stands for "Anno Fordi" or "After Ford". It starts counting from 1908 AD, the year when Ford launched the Model T into production. In the book, people say "Ford!", instead of "God!", and the cross has been cut down into a T. It's meant to be humorous. But the point here is that a society built around mass production might end up dating itself by it. The case is not so different for us; instead of mass production, we have AI, and we haven't picked our 1908 yet. There are a few obvious candidates, such as Turing's 1950 paper, which asked the gold question: can machines think? The 1956 Dartmouth workshop, which coined the term "Artificial Intelligence". We then have ChatGPT in November 2022, which accelerated a lot…

items.summary: RIDArena (Rogue Internal Deployment Arena) is an AI control evaluation environment that simulates an AI lab’s R&D infrastructure. Researchers can use it to study how an agent can covertly sabotage the lab’s monitoring system and deploy another rogue agent without oversight. RIDArena can support sabotage, control, and monitor evaluations in a highly configurable R&D environment. These evaluations are increasingly important as AI labs assess the risks posed by their models. Existing settings such as LinuxArena lack the complexity and realism needed to replicate recent incidents or test potential future catastrophic scenarios. Monitoring can fail when suspicious behavior goes unnoticed or when the monitoring infrastructure itself is compromised. RIDArena lets researchers study both failure modes and compare the effectiveness of different…

items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. items.summary: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has made significant progress in explaining the internal computations of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, these advances have yet to demonstrate comparable success in explaining the decision-making processes of LLM-based agents. We find that a linear probe trained on the last prompt token can predict hallucinations before generation begins (0.80 AUC) and steering along a probe direction corrects 85\% of hallucinations, but disrupts 7\% of valid actions. items.summary: Subliminal learning is the phenomenon where a language model can learn a behavior from semantically unrelated training data. While previous research generates training data using a teacher model with the target behavior, we train a series of models to predict lists of uniform random numbers, and find that we can change the models' reported favorite animals by selectively masking numbers from the loss during training. This works best on models that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens. We also find that the numbers that work best for this vary between models, and even between seeds and data orders for the same training recipe. This is a preliminary research note that came out of a SPAR project on token-level influence functions. We expect these results to hold up, but haven't explored all possibilities and we're unsure why this…

items.summary: Efficient and secure beam alignment is essential for mmWave communication systems. However, existing deep learning (DL)-based beam alignment methods often neglect causal relationships between inputs and outputs, resulting in limited interpretability, poor generalization, and excessive beam sweeping. Moreover, these DL solutions are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where small perturbations in received power measurements can mislead beam classifiers. To overcome these issues, we propose a causally-aware DL framework integrating causal discovery into beam alignment. A two-stage causal beam selection algorithm learns a Bayesian graph capturing dependencies between received signal strength indicators (RSSI) as inputs and the optimal beam index as the target variable, then uses it to select a minimal set of relevant input features for the…

items.summary: A runtime signature, captured without weights or response text, achieves 99.3% pair separation across 53 models. Using only ordinary inference requests, no access to weights and without reading response text, I extracted the individual fingerprints for 53 open-weight models (0.5B to 9B) from 13 families as runtime signatures with a 99.3% model pair separation (1,368 of 1,378). Under baseline identification and verification testing, a Claim Check against all other registered models had an AUC of 0.9997 and equal error rate of 0.5%, while held-out sessions matched their own model's signature 94.4% of the time (202 of 214), with the correct model in the top three presented every time. items.summary: Neural networks are powerful predictors, yet their opacity limits their usefulness in science, where the goal is explanation rather than mere prediction. In neuroscience, for example, deep encoding models accurately predict brain activity in response to natural stimuli, but struggle to reveal which stimulus features drive those predictions. Here we introduce interpretable weight-space programming (iWSP), a method in which an LLM agent iteratively builds interpretable models by explicitly programming their weights and features in code, without gradient-based training (backpropagation). Without backpropagation to tune parameters, the agent must draw on its prior knowledge and reason over previous trials to hypothesize, hand-craft, and refine human-interpretable computations mirroring the workflow of a human scientist. items.summary: We propose a bound preserving finite-volume scheme for a coupled system of partial differential equations with nonlinear, nonlocal drift. The main contribution of this work is twofold: $(1)$ we show that the proposed scheme preserves physically motivated bounds; $(2)$ we prove that the scheme is well-posed and leads to a sequence of approximate solutions converging to the weak solution of the original problem. This setting is motivated by questions related to morphology formation in organic solar cells.

There was already some tension in our weekly meetings: I often voiced my dissatisfaction with the pace of academia, my interests had been drifting away from theirs, and, most of all, we disagreed on the severity of the risks AI posed. When I walked into the room, they told me something I would have loved to hear months earlier: “We think it’s time to get you started on some research.” All I could say was, “I think it’s a little too late for that.” For months, I had been proposing projects that bridged my interests with theirs, such as running studies that treated humans and LLMs as equal subjects, but they were usually turned down for not being “exciting…

items.summary: Inspired by https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/xPrL2xF9iYWpPmu6B/my-empathy-is-rarely-kind I find myself confused about empathy. I wrote this to try and deconfuse myself. Let's take the example case of "posting bad political takes on the internet." When I see someone doing this, it bothers me. But then I remind myself of times that I've posted stuff that I later thought was bad. This establishes a certain baseline of empathy. But then I hit a problem: when I think back on those times, I feel shame. So though I get it, it basically justifies me feeling negative things towards them. If I feel negative towards myself for those things, it seems fair for me to send that their way. But this isn't really fair, right? I'm judging them by my own values, not theirs. There are things I've said online that I do stand behind. Presumably they feel that…

items.summary: Reinforcement learning has enabled robust humanoid locomotion, yet training recipes (rewards, architectures, hyperparameters) remain hard to reuse across robots with different native joint coordinates, since policies output native joint angles while action scales, bounds, gains, and penalties are defined in those robot-specific coordinates. items.summary: IEEE 802.11ax introduced orthogonal frequency division multiple access (OFDMA) to improve channel utilization through concurrent multi-user transmissions. For effective uplink (UL) scheduling, the access point (AP) requires timely knowledge of buffered traffic at the stations (STAs). Explicit buffer-status polling provides this, yet each polling round can query only as many STAs as there are resource units (RUs). Scheduled-access, random-access, activity-based, and learning-based schemes address this buffer-status acquisition problem differently and have generally been evaluated in isolation under different conditions, so it remains unclear how they compare across time-sensitive workloads. items.summary: arXiv:2611.15744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parameterized-action MDPs (PAMDPs) ask an agent to choose a discrete action together with continuous parameters whose meaning depends on that choice. items.summary: arXiv:2611.16694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When language models revise a decision after another agent disagrees, neither reversal counts nor final accuracy shows whether they are fixing mistakes or abandoning correct answers.
